--- title: "Class imbalance" description: "When one answer is rare, a model can be right 95% of the time by never giving it. Sensitivity, specificity and precision count the two kinds of mistake apart, and show that rebalancing the training data does no more than move the threshold." order: 5 categories: [assumptions, class-imbalance, metrics] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Accuracy rewards a model that ignores the rare class Some of the outcomes marine scientists most want to predict are rare: a protected species in a haul, a harmful algal bloom, a bleaching event. When one answer is much rarer than the other the classes are **imbalanced**, and a model can score well by never giving the rare answer. If a species is caught at 5% of stations, calling it absent everywhere is right 95% of the time and finds nothing. This page counts the rare cases such a model actually finds, and tests the usual fix. [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd#a-threshold-turns-a-probability-into-yes-or-no) turned a predicted probability into yes or no with a threshold, and named the two ways that answer can be wrong: a false alarm says yes where the truth is no, and a miss says no where the truth is yes. It also warned that for a rare species the probabilities may never reach the default threshold of 0.5. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Three measures count misses and false alarms apart Accuracy adds up both kinds of right answer. Three measures keep them apart, each the share of one group of cases: - **Sensitivity**, also called recall: of the cases that are truly yes, the share called yes. Misses lower it. - **Specificity**: of the cases that are truly no, the share called no. False alarms lower it. - **Precision**: of the cases called yes, the share that are truly yes. False alarms lower it too, and when yes is rare they easily outnumber the true yeses: with 5 yeses in 100 cases, calling one no in ten yes gives about 10 false alarms. When nearly every case is no, accuracy is mostly specificity, so a model can miss every yes and still look good. ::: {.diagram} ![The same twenty cases, four truly yes and sixteen truly no, with six called yes. Sensitivity is the share of true yeses called yes, lowered by misses. Specificity is the share of true noes called no, lowered by false alarms. Precision is the share of yes calls that are true, also lowered by false alarms.](img/three-measures.svg){fig-alt="Three cards show the same twenty cases in two rows: four truly yes, drawn filled, and sixteen truly no, drawn open. A dashed box marks the six the model called yes: three true yeses and three noes. One true yes lies outside the box. Sensitivity, lowered by misses: of the four true yeses, three were called yes and one, the miss, was not; 3 of 4. Specificity, lowered by false alarms: of the sixteen true noes, thirteen were called no and three, the false alarms, sit in the box; 13 of 16. Precision, lowered by false alarms: of the six yes calls, three are true and three are false alarms; 3 of 6. A note says accuracy, 16 of 20, hides the miss, because when yeses are few it mostly counts the noes."} ::: ## Rebalancing evens out the classes before fitting The common fix for imbalance is to change the data the model is fitted to, so that both answers are equally common. **Downsampling** drops cases of the common class at random until they match the rare one. **Upsampling** copies cases of the rare class at random until they match the common one. **SMOTE**, a popular variant of upsampling, makes new rare cases between pairs of real ones instead of copying them. In R these are recipe steps from the `themis` package, so they change only the stations a model is fitted to. The stations it is scored on keep their real mix, as they must: upsampling the whole survey before splitting would put copies of the same station on both sides of the split, a kind of [information leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd). ## Worked example The outcome is `rare_species`, a second species caught at only a few stations. The model is logistic regression on the six inputs, each entering the log-odds as a straight line: with so few presences, squared terms would leave too little data for each coefficient. The split by site is that of [Linearity and nonlinearity](linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd), and the scores come from cross-validation by site, introduced in [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). One round of ten folds holds only a few presences in each, so the round is repeated five times, and every training station is predicted five times by models that never saw its site. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) folds <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = site_id, v = 10, repeats = 5) no_rebalancing <- recipe( rare_species ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> # dummies before rebalancing, so a fit that lacks a seabed type still runs step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) recipes <- list( "No rebalancing" = no_rebalancing, "Downsampling" = no_rebalancing |> step_downsample(rare_species), "Upsampling" = no_rebalancing |> step_upsample(rare_species) ) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True) folds = [fold for r in range(5) for fold in GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=r) .split(train, groups=train["site_id"])] numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical present = (train["rare_species"] == "yes").to_numpy() model = Pipeline([ ("recipe", ColumnTransformer([ # scaling leaves an unpenalised fit unchanged; it helps the solver converge ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric), # every level listed, so a fit that lacks a seabed type still runs ("categorical", OneHotEncoder( categories=[list(train[c].cat.categories) for c in categorical], drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ])), ("model", LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=5000)), ]) # scikit-learn has no rebalancing step, so the fitting rows are resampled by hand def rebalance(rows, training, rng): yes, no = rows[present[rows]], rows[~present[rows]] if training == "Downsampling": no = rng.choice(no, size=len(yes), replace=False) if training == "Upsampling": yes = rng.choice(yes, size=len(no), replace=True) return np.concatenate([yes, no]) ``` ::: ::: The 598 training stations include only 29 with the rare species, 4.8% of them. ### The default threshold calls almost no station present Each recipe is fitted in every fold, and its predictions for the left-out sites are kept. `calls()` is the function of [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd), with the three measures added. The counts cover all five repeats, so each station is counted five times. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions <- recipes |> imap(\(recipe, training) { workflow(recipe, logistic_reg()) |> fit_resamples(folds, control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |> collect_predictions() |> mutate(training = training) }) |> list_rbind() calls <- function(probability, truth, threshold) { called <- probability >= threshold present <- truth == "yes" tibble(threshold, called_present = sum(called), false_alarms = sum(called & !present), misses = sum(!called & present), sensitivity = mean(called[present]), specificity = mean(!called[!present]), precision = mean(present[called]), accuracy = mean(called == present)) } at_default <- predictions |> summarise(calls(.pred_yes, rare_species, 0.5), .by = training) at_default |> mutate(across(sensitivity:accuracy, \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|training | threshold| called_present| false_alarms| misses| sensitivity| specificity| precision| accuracy| |:--------------|---------:|--------------:|------------:|------:|-----------:|-----------:|---------:|--------:| |No rebalancing | 0.5| 2| 2| 145| 0.000| 0.999| 0.000| 0.951| |Downsampling | 0.5| 1038| 940| 47| 0.676| 0.670| 0.094| 0.670| |Upsampling | 0.5| 923| 819| 41| 0.717| 0.712| 0.113| 0.712|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(123) pieces = [] for training in ["No rebalancing", "Downsampling", "Upsampling"]: for fitting, scoring in folds: kept = rebalance(fitting, training, rng) fitted = model.fit(train.loc[kept, predictors], present[kept]) pieces.append(pd.DataFrame({ "training": training, "present": present[scoring], "pred_yes": fitted.predict_proba( train.loc[scoring, predictors])[:, 1], })) predictions = pd.concat(pieces, ignore_index=True) def calls(probability, is_present, threshold): called = probability >= threshold return { "threshold": threshold, "called_present": int(called.sum()), "false_alarms": int((called & ~is_present).sum()), "misses": int((~called & is_present).sum()), "sensitivity": called[is_present].mean(), "specificity": (~called[~is_present]).mean(), "precision": is_present[called].mean() if called.any() else np.nan, "accuracy": (called == is_present).mean(), } at_default = pd.DataFrame([ {"training": training, **calls(group["pred_yes"].to_numpy(), group["present"].to_numpy(), 0.5)} for training, group in predictions.groupby("training", sort=False) ]) at_default.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | training | threshold | called_present | false_alarms | misses | sensitivity | specificity | precision | accuracy | |:---------------|------------:|-----------------:|---------------:|---------:|--------------:|--------------:|------------:|-----------:| | No rebalancing | 0.5 | 0 | 0 | 130 | 0 | 1 | nan | 0.955 | | Downsampling | 0.5 | 1218 | 1138 | 50 | 0.615 | 0.585 | 0.066 | 0.587 | | Upsampling | 0.5 | 993 | 916 | 53 | 0.592 | 0.666 | 0.078 | 0.663 | ::: ::: ::: Without rebalancing, the highest probability logistic regression gives any station is 0.52, so the default threshold calls only 2 of the 2990 predictions present and catches 0 of the 145 presences. Its sensitivity is 0 and its accuracy 95%: reported as accuracy alone, a model that finds nothing would sound like a success. Both kinds of rebalancing raise the sensitivity to about 0.7, so most presences are now found. The price is the specificity: about 31% of the absences become false alarms, and accuracy falls to about 69%. Precision stays low whichever way: about one station in 9 called present by the upsampled model holds the species. ### Upsampling gives the same answers as a lower threshold Lowering the threshold is the other way to call more stations present. The curve below applies every threshold from 0 to 1 to the predictions made without rebalancing: each point is a sensitivity and specificity the same probabilities can give. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plain_predictions <- filter(predictions, training == "No rebalancing") by_threshold <- function(threshold) { calls(plain_predictions$.pred_yes, plain_predictions$rare_species, threshold) } curve <- map(seq(0, 1, by = 0.002), by_threshold) |> list_rbind() bind_rows( "Upsampling, threshold 0.5" = select(upsampled, -training), "No rebalancing, threshold = prevalence" = by_threshold(prevalence), .id = "model" ) |> mutate(across(threshold:accuracy, \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | threshold| called_present| false_alarms| misses| sensitivity| specificity| precision| accuracy| |:--------------------------------------|---------:|--------------:|------------:|------:|-----------:|-----------:|---------:|--------:| |Upsampling, threshold 0.5 | 0.500| 923| 819| 41| 0.717| 0.712| 0.113| 0.712| |No rebalancing, threshold = prevalence | 0.048| 923| 819| 41| 0.717| 0.712| 0.113| 0.712|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} plain_predictions = predictions[predictions["training"] == "No rebalancing"] prevalence = present.mean() def by_threshold(threshold): return calls(plain_predictions["pred_yes"].to_numpy(), plain_predictions["present"].to_numpy(), threshold) curve = pd.DataFrame([by_threshold(t) for t in np.arange(0, 1.001, 0.002)]) upsampled = at_default[at_default["training"] == "Upsampling"] pd.DataFrame([ {"model": "Upsampling, threshold 0.5", **upsampled.drop(columns="training").iloc[0].to_dict()}, {"model": "No rebalancing, threshold = prevalence", **by_threshold(prevalence)}, ]).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | threshold | called_present | false_alarms | misses | sensitivity | specificity | precision | accuracy | |:---------------------------------------|------------:|-----------------:|---------------:|---------:|--------------:|--------------:|------------:|-----------:| | Upsampling, threshold 0.5 | 0.5 | 993 | 916 | 53 | 0.592 | 0.666 | 0.078 | 0.663 | | No rebalancing, threshold = prevalence | 0.045 | 981 | 907 | 56 | 0.569 | 0.67 | 0.075 | 0.665 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rebalanced <- filter(at_default, training != "No rebalancing") ggplot(curve, aes(specificity, sensitivity)) + geom_path(colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) + geom_point(data = by_threshold(prevalence), shape = 1, size = 6, stroke = 1.2) + geom_point(data = rebalanced, aes(colour = training), size = 3.6) + geom_point(data = plain, shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(Downsampling = ml_palette[["blue"]], Upsampling = ml_palette[["orange"]])) + scale_x_reverse() + labs(x = "Specificity", y = "Sensitivity", colour = NULL, title = "Rebalancing moves along the threshold's curve, not above it", subtitle = paste("Grey: logistic regression without rebalancing,", "at every threshold")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sensitivity against specificity for logistic regression on the rare species, from cross-validation by site. The grey curve is the model fitted without rebalancing, at every threshold. The cross is that model at the default threshold of 0.5, and the open circle at a threshold equal to the share of stations with the species. The coloured points are the downsampled and upsampled models at 0.5.](class-imbalance_files/figure-html/fig-curve-1.png){#fig-curve fig-alt='A plot of sensitivity from 0 to 1 against specificity running from 1 on the left to 0 on the right. A grey curve rises steeply from the bottom left corner and flattens towards the top right. A black cross sits in the bottom left corner, at specificity 1 and sensitivity 0. An orange point for upsampling sits on the curve at specificity 0.71 and sensitivity 0.72, over an open circle for the model without rebalancing at a threshold equal to the prevalence. A blue point for downsampling, at specificity 0.67 and sensitivity 0.68, sits below the curve.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: Upsampling at 0.5 and no rebalancing at a threshold of 0.048, the share of training stations with the species, are the same point: a sensitivity of 0.717 against 0.717, and a specificity of 0.712 against 0.712. The odds from [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) explain the match. Copying each presence about 20 times multiplies every station's odds of presence by about 20, which leaves the order of the stations as it was. A probability of 0.5 after upsampling is therefore one near the prevalence before it. Downsampling lands below the curve. At its specificity of 0.67, a lower threshold on the model without rebalancing reaches a sensitivity of 0.75, where downsampling reaches 0.68. Each downsampled fit keeps only as many absences as there are presences, about one absence in 20, so it learns the absences from far fewer stations. ### Rebalanced probabilities overstate the chance of presence A predicted probability should match the rate of the event: of the stations given 0.1, about one in ten should hold the species. The table compares each model's average predicted probability with the share of its predictions where the species was present. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predictions |> summarise(average_probability = round(mean(.pred_yes), 3), share_present = round(mean(rare_species == "yes"), 3), .by = training) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|training | average_probability| share_present| |:--------------|-------------------:|-------------:| |No rebalancing | 0.048| 0.048| |Downsampling | 0.362| 0.048| |Upsampling | 0.342| 0.048|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} (predictions.groupby("training", sort=False) .agg(average_probability=("pred_yes", "mean"), share_present=("present", "mean")) .round(3).reset_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | training | average_probability | share_present | |:---------------|----------------------:|----------------:| | No rebalancing | 0.046 | 0.045 | | Downsampling | 0.446 | 0.045 | | Upsampling | 0.395 | 0.045 | ::: ::: ::: Without rebalancing, the average probability, 0.048, matches the share of stations with the species, as it should. After upsampling it averages 0.34, about 7 times too high: of the 239 predictions above 0.8, only 18% are stations with the species. A rebalanced model can still rank stations, but its probabilities are no longer chances. To report "a 10% chance of the species here", leave the data alone and move the threshold. ## A threshold set from the costs does the work of rebalancing Neither rebalancing nor a lower threshold makes the model better at telling presence from absence. Both choose where on the same curve to work, and the threshold does it without discarding stations or distorting the probabilities. Where to work depends on what each mistake costs: if a miss leaves a protected species unprotected, work far up the curve and accept the false alarms; if every station called present sends out a dive team, work lower down. At a sensitivity of about 0.7 here, each presence found comes with about 8 false alarms. [Classification performance measures](../07-validation/classification-metrics.qmd) summarises a whole curve in one number, so that models can be compared before a threshold is chosen, and [Choosing measures that match the objective](../07-validation/choosing-a-metric.qmd) turns the costs of the two mistakes into a threshold. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - With a rare class, accuracy mostly measures a model's success on the common class. Logistic regression without rebalancing was 95% accurate and found 0 of 145 presences. - **Sensitivity**, **specificity** and **precision** count misses and false alarms apart; report them, not accuracy alone. - Rebalancing, done in the recipe so that it changes only the stations a model is fitted to, moves a model along the curve the threshold traces. Upsampling at 0.5 matched no rebalancing at a threshold of 0.048, and downsampling landed below the curve. - A rebalanced model's probabilities are no longer chances: after upsampling they averaged 0.34 where the species was at 4.8% of stations. - Choose the threshold from the cost of each mistake. With a rare class, precision stays low wherever it is set. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. `step_downsample(rare_species, under_ratio = 3)` keeps three absences for each presence. Add it as a fourth recipe: where does its point land on @fig-curve? 2. Replace `logistic_reg()` with `rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification")`, as in [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd), and redraw @fig-curve. Does upsampling still land on the forest's own curve?
